chapter_title: The Factory Method Pattern: Decoupling Object Creation

screens.title: Factory Method Pattern
screens.subtitle: Deferring object creation to reduce coupling and improve extensibility

narration.text: In this lesson we explore the Factory Method, a creational pattern that helps you decouple client code from concrete classes. Many programs directly instantiate classes and then must change every client when a new concrete type appears. The Factory Method fixes that by defining a method that creates objects and letting subclasses decide the concrete type. You will learn the essential participants — Product, ConcreteProduct, Creator, and ConcreteCreator — and see how they fit together in Java. Through a document-processing example and a logger factory exercise, you'll practice replacing if/else instantiation with polymorphic creation. We'll also highlight common mistakes, like overusing factories or confusing the pattern with a simple static factory. By the end of the lesson you should be able to identify where object creation is tightly coupled, refactor it into a Creator hierarchy, and add new product types by adding classes rather than altering existing client logic. Think about a recent class in your code that other classes directly instantiate; could deferring that creation make your code easier to extend?

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Define a factory method in a Creator and let subclasses return concrete Products. This moves the new operation into a class hierarchy so clients depend on interfaces, not concrete classes.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Factory Method Pattern
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Factory Method

Learn why deferring instantiation to subclasses makes your Java code open to extension and closed to modification.

In this lesson: understand participants, refactor a tightly coupled example, and implement a logger factory exercise to practice.
Why it matters

Directly creating concrete objects scatters knowledge of specific classes across clients. The Factory Method groups creation logic into a Creator hierarchy so clients work with the Product interface only.

Problem
Tight coupling via new operators and if/else chains.
Pattern
Creator declares factory method; ConcreteCreators return ConcreteProducts.
Benefit
Add products by adding classes, not by modifying clients.
Visual concept
Creator
Declares factory method; uses Product in operations.
Product
Interface or abstract class for created objects.
ConcreteCreator
Overrides factory to return a ConcreteProduct.
ConcreteProduct
Implements Product behavior.
Hierarchy of responsibility
Explore Key Topics
Tight Coupling
Why direct new calls scatter knowledge of classes.
Pattern Roles
Product, Creator, Concrete variants and their responsibilities.
Extending safely
Add product types by adding classes, not editing clients.

screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this first objectives slide you should be able to explain the problem of tight coupling that arises when clients instantiate concrete classes directly. You'll describe the Factory Method as a way to defer creation to subclasses and identify each participant: Product, ConcreteProduct, Creator, and ConcreteCreator. You will also start to recognize where to apply the pattern in existing Java code, such as a document processor or logging system. For each objective, you should practice naming a concrete example from your own code that uses direct construction and think through how a Creator hierarchy would replace those new calls. This makes the objectives concrete and actionable. Finally, you'll understand why this pattern matters to maintainability: it helps you add new types without changing client logic, which aligns with the Open/Closed Principle. A short self-check is to list a class you would refactor into a Product and sketch a corresponding Creator that returns it.

screens.title: What is the Factory Method?
screens.subtitle: A definition that focuses on deferring instantiation to subclasses

narration.text: The Factory Method is a creational pattern that defines an interface for creating an object but lets subclasses decide which class to instantiate. Put simply, instead of writing 'new ConcreteType' in client code, you declare a factory method that returns the Product type. ConcreteCreator subclasses override that factory to return specific ConcreteProducts. This matters because it moves the decision about which class to use out of the client and into a controlled hierarchy. A concrete example in the chapter is a Document system where a DocumentCreator defines createDocument and ConcreteCreators like WordDocumentCreator return WordDocument or PdfDocument. A common misconception is to think a static factory method that accepts a type string is the same pattern; the Factory Method specifically relies on inheritance and polymorphism to defer creation. When you apply it, you get clearer separation of concerns: clients use Product operations without needing to know construction details. Consider whether your current code anticipates new product types. If it does and client code needs to remain unchanged when these types are added, the Factory Method is a strong candidate. How would you name the Creator and Product in your codebase?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Factory Method defers object instantiation to subclasses by defining a factory method that returns a Product interface.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › What is the Factory Method?
Definition

Factory Method explained

The Factory Method declares a method for creating a Product and lets subclasses decide which ConcreteProduct to return. This moves 'new' out of client code.

Quick cards
Product: interface or abstract type that clients use.
Creator: declares the factory method and may use the Product in operations.
ConcreteCreator: overrides factory to return a specific ConcreteProduct.
Analogy

Think of a restaurant menu. The menu (Creator) defines a dish category. Different chefs (ConcreteCreators) prepare a specific dish (ConcreteProduct) that conforms to the category (Product). Diners order by category, not by chef implementation.

Common misconception
A static factory that switches on a type string is not the GoF Factory Method. The Factory Method uses subclassing and polymorphism to decide the concrete type.
Key Takeaway

Deferring creation via a factory method reduces client knowledge of concrete classes and enables safe extension.

screens.title: Problem: Tight coupling via direct instantiation
screens.subtitle: See why if/else construction makes code brittle

narration.text: Start with a common, naive approach that many developers take: choosing implementations with conditional logic and direct construction. The chapter gives a DocumentProcessor that inspects a type string and then uses new to construct WordDocument or PdfDocument. This seems straightforward, but it embeds knowledge of every concrete class into the processor. If you add HtmlDocument, you must edit the processor and add another branch. That violates the Open/Closed Principle: the processor is not closed for modification. It also scatters construction logic across clients, making changes error-prone and tests harder to write. An additional issue is that the client must import or reference concrete types, increasing coupling and reducing reuse. Contrast this with deferring creation to a Creator that returns a Product; then the processor calls creator. createDocument and remains unchanged when new types arrive. A typical misconception is to assume conditional creation is acceptable for small projects; while often true initially, it becomes a maintenance liability as types grow. Try to identify code in your own projects where a type switch or series of if/else statements decides which class to instantiate. That is a candidate for factory refactoring.

keyIdea.title: Why refactor
keyIdea.text: Conditional new-calls lead to scattered creation logic and violate Open/Closed; move creation into Creator subclasses to make additions non-invasive.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Tight coupling example
Naive code
// Naive approach: tight coupling
public class DocumentProcessor {
  public void processDocument(String type) {
    if (type.equals("Word")) {
      WordDocument doc = new WordDocument();
      doc.open();
      doc.save();
    } else if (type.equals("PDF")) {
      PdfDocument doc = new PdfDocument();
      doc.open();
      doc.print();
    }
    // ... more document types
  }
}
Why this is fragile
  • Every new Document type requires editing the processor and adding imports.
  • Client code knows concrete class names and constructors, increasing coupling.
  • Violates Open/Closed Principle: the class is not closed to modification.
Common mistake
Assuming conditional factories are fine for growth; they often become maintenance headaches.
Pro tip

If creation logic changes together with product details, centralize it in a Creator to limit modification points.

screens.title: Product and ConcreteProducts in Java
screens.subtitle: Define the Product interface and concrete implementations

narration.text: A core step in applying the Factory Method is to define a Product abstraction that clients will use. In the chapter example, Product is a Document interface with open, close and save methods. ConcreteProducts implement that interface, such as WordDocument and PdfDocument. The chapter shows simple implementations where each method prints a message, which is ideal for an early refactor and unit testing. Defining a Product interface ensures that clients and Creator operations call a stable A P I, regardless of the concrete type returned. One nuance is that concrete products may have behavior that only makes sense for that format — for instance, PdfDocument might implement print differently — but they must still adhere to the Product contract. A common misconception is to add product-specific operations directly to the interface; resist that. Keep the Product interface focused and, when necessary, use type-specific adapters or separate interfaces. As an example, the chapter's WordDocument and PdfDocument implementations show how you can adhere to a common contract while providing different internals. After writing these classes, compile and run simple calls to verify the polymorphic behavior.

keyIdea.title: Product contract
keyIdea.text: Create a tight, useful Product interface and implement concrete classes that satisfy that contract while encapsulating format-specific behavior internally.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Product & ConcreteProducts
Product Interface
// Product Interface
public interface Document {
  void open();
  void close();
  void save();
}
Keep the interface minimal and focused on what clients need. Implement details inside concrete classes.
Concrete Products
public class WordDocument implements Document {
  @Override
  public void open() { System.out.println("Opening Word Document."); }
  @Override
  public void close() { System.out.println("Closing Word Document."); }
  @Override
  public void save() { System.out.println("Saving Word Document."); }
}

public class PdfDocument implements Document {
  @Override
  public void open() { System.out.println("Opening PDF Document."); }
  @Override
  public void close() { System.out.println("Closing PDF Document."); }
  @Override
  public void save() { System.out.println("Saving PDF Document."); }
}
Concrete implementations can differ internally but must respect the Document contract so clients can use them interchangeably.
Key Takeaway

A small, stable Product interface is the anchor of a flexible Creator hierarchy.

Misconception

Do not add product-specific methods to the shared interface; prefer separate interfaces or adapters when needed.

screens.title: Creator: the factory method and operations
screens.subtitle: Creator declares the factory method and uses the Product in operations

narration.text: The Creator is an abstract class or interface that declares the factory method, typically returning the Product type. In our document example, DocumentCreator defines an abstract createDocument method and a concrete operation processNewDocument that calls createDocument and then uses the document. The important architectural point is the inversion: Creator contains operations that work with Product but delegates the actual instantiation to subclasses. This lets operations in the Creator remain unchanged even as ConcreteCreators provide different products. The chapter's processNewDocument shows open, save and close being invoked on the produced Document; because the Creator operates against the Document interface, any ConcreteProduct will work. When designing Creator, think about which operations belong there versus which are the responsibility of the product. Avoid putting product-specific behavior into Creator; keep Creator focused on composition and orchestration. A typical pitfall is to leak concrete construction details from a Creator subclass back into client code; ensure the Creator's public A P I hides creation choices. Creator: the factory method and operations means creator defines the factory method and may implement operations that use the product, relying on polymorphism for flexibility.. In practical terms, creator declares the factory method and uses the product in operations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Creator role
keyIdea.text: Creator defines the factory method and may implement operations that use the Product, relying on polymorphism for flexibility.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Creator Architecture
Creator Abstract Class
// Creator Abstract Class
public abstract class DocumentCreator {
  // The factory method
  public abstract Document createDocument();

  // Other operations that use the created document
  public void processNewDocument() {
    Document doc = createDocument(); // Call the factory method
    doc.open();
    doc.save();
    doc.close();
    System.out.println("Document processed successfully.");
  }
}
Architectural notes
  • Creator contains orchestration logic that works with Product methods.
  • Creation is deferred: subclasses supply the concrete Product without changing Creator's operations.
  • Clients interact with Creator or Product, not with ConcreteProduct constructors.
Key Takeaway

Put common workflows in Creator and let subclasses decide the specific Product returned.

screens.title: ConcreteCreators and client usage
screens.subtitle: ConcreteCreators supply specific products; the client uses Creator interfaces

narration.text: ConcreteCreators are simple classes that extend the Creator and override the factory method to return a ConcreteProduct. In the chapter, WordDocumentCreator returns new WordDocument and PdfDocumentCreator returns new PdfDocument. The client code then instantiates a specific Creator and calls its operation, such as processNewDocument, without ever calling new on concrete document types. This is the critical decoupling point. The Application example shows a main method creating a WordDocumentCreator and a PdfDocumentCreator and calling processNewDocument on each. Adding a new product requires creating ExcelDocument and ExcelDocumentCreator; the Application remains unchanged except for choosing the new Creator. A misconception to watch for is letting concrete creation leak into client code; keep creators consistent and let client choose the desired Creator, not the product internals. Use the Creator type in method signatures where possible so callers program to the abstraction, not a concrete factory subclass. ConcreteCreators and client usage means concretecreators override the factory method to return concrete product instances; clients interact with creator interfaces, not with concrete products.. In practical terms, concretecreators supply specific products; the client uses creator interfaces. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: ConcreteCreators
keyIdea.text: ConcreteCreators override the factory method to return concrete product instances; clients interact with Creator interfaces, not with concrete products.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › ConcreteCreators & Client
Concrete Creators
// Concrete Creators
public class WordDocumentCreator extends DocumentCreator {
  @Override
  public Document createDocument() {
    return new WordDocument();
  }
}

public class PdfDocumentCreator extends DocumentCreator {
  @Override
  public Document createDocument() {
    return new PdfDocument();
  }
}
Client Example
// Client code
public class Application {
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    DocumentCreator wordCreator = new WordDocumentCreator();
    wordCreator.processNewDocument(); // Creates and processes a WordDocument

    DocumentCreator pdfCreator = new PdfDocumentCreator();
    pdfCreator.processNewDocument(); // Creates and processes a PdfDocument
  }
}
Key Takeaway

Clients work with Creator and Product abstractions; ConcreteCreators are the only classes that know about concrete products.

Misconception

Don't let client code call new ConcreteProduct directly; choose a Creator and invoke its operations instead.

screens.title: Factory Method vs Simple/Static Factory
screens.subtitle: Understand the difference and when to prefer each

narration.text: It's common to confuse the Factory Method with a simple static factory. The Simple Factory is typically a static method that checks an input parameter and returns different concrete types. That is convenient but often violates the Open/Closed Principle because adding a new product requires changing the static method. The Factory Method, by contrast, uses subclassing: Creator declares a factory method and ConcreteCreators override it to return a particular product. This lets you add new creators without modifying existing ones or client code that depends on the Creator abstraction. A concrete example: a static logger factory might take a string and return ConsoleLogger or FileLogger. That approach centralizes creation but still needs edits when adding a DatabaseLogger. The Factory Method would place the responsibility into separate factories like ConsoleLoggerFactory and FileLoggerFactory, allowing growth through new classes. A common tradeoff is complexity: the Factory Method introduces more classes and abstractions, which can be unnecessary for small, stable sets of products. Choose the simpler static factory when you truly do not expect new types, and prefer Factory Method when extension and polymorphic behavior matter.

keyIdea.title: Pattern choice
keyIdea.text: Use a static factory when product types are stable; prefer Factory Method when you need polymorphic extension without editing central switch logic.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Factory Method vs Simple Factory
Simple / Static Factory
  • Single static method returns different concrete types based on input.
  • Easy to implement but must be edited for new products.
  • Tends to centralize creation logic into one class.
Factory Method (GoF)
  • Uses inheritance: Creator declares factory, ConcreteCreators override it.
  • Add new types by adding classes, not modifying existing factories.
  • Supports polymorphism and aligns with Open/Closed Principle.
When to choose which
Prefer static factory when types are stable and you want simplicity.
Prefer Factory Method when you expect frequent extension and want polymorphic factories.

screens.title: Advantages of the Factory Method
screens.subtitle: Decoupling, extensibility, flexibility and centralized creation

narration.text: The chapter lists concrete benefits of using the Factory Method. First, decoupling: client code depends on a Product interface rather than concrete classes, which reduces compile-time dependencies and makes mocking easier in tests. Second, extensibility: to introduce a new product, add a ConcreteProduct and a ConcreteCreator; existing code does not change. Third, flexibility: ConcreteCreators can return specialized or wrapped products, for example a SecurePdfDocument returned by a SecurePdfDocumentCreator, which adds behavior without changing client code. Fourth, centralized creation logic: construction details stay in creators, making changes easier to manage, such as injecting configuration or applying a shared initialization policy. These benefits come with costs: more classes and indirection. The pattern is most valuable when creation logic is likely to change or when multiple families of products exist. A good exercise is to identify a real factory point in your code and list what would change if you added one or two new product types. If adding a type requires touching many clients, the Factory Method will likely help. Advantages of the Factory Method means factory method reduces coupling, supports extension by adding classes, enables flexible return types, and centralizes creation logic for easier maintenance.. In practical terms, decoupling, extensibility, flexibility and centralized creation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Benefits summary
keyIdea.text: Factory Method reduces coupling, supports extension by adding classes, enables flexible return types, and centralizes creation logic for easier maintenance.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Advantages
Decoupling

Clients program to the Product interface and do not need to import concrete classes. This reduces dependencies and simplifies testing.

Extensibility

Add a new ConcreteProduct and ConcreteCreator to extend behavior without modifying existing code.

Flexibility

ConcreteCreators can return decorated or specialized products, enabling variation without client changes.

Centralized creation

Creation logic lives in creators, making it easier to change initialization policies or add logging and instrumentation.

Tradeoff

The pattern adds classes and indirection. Use it when extension, polymorphism, or centralized creation adds measurable value.

screens.title: Adding a new product type safely
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step: add ExcelDocument without modifying clients

narration.text: One of the most convincing demonstrations of the Factory Method is how it lets you add new product types without changing client code. The chapter uses the hypothetical ExcelDocument. To add it: first implement ExcelDocument that implements Document. Next, create ExcelDocumentCreator that extends DocumentCreator and overrides createDocument to return new ExcelDocument. Finally, use new ExcelDocumentCreator where you need Excel support. The Application or other clients do not require changes to their processNewDocument logic. This workflow directly shows support for the Open/Closed Principle: the system is open to extension by adding classes, but closed to modification of existing creators and clients. A common misstep is to add product-specific logic into DocumentCreator or into existing ConcreteCreators; instead, prefer a new ConcreteCreator. If the creation needs parameters, expose them through the ConcreteCreator constructor or factory configuration, avoiding pollution of the Creator's public A P I. After implementing, run the processNewDocument flow and confirm that ExcelDocument methods execute as expected. This simple sequence of class additions is the practical core of the pattern's value. Adding a new product type safely means add a new concreteproduct and concretecreator; clients remain unchanged, demonstrating open/closed adherence.. In practical terms, step-by-step: add exceldocument without modifying clients. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Safe extension
keyIdea.text: Add a new ConcreteProduct and ConcreteCreator; clients remain unchanged, demonstrating Open/Closed adherence.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Add New Product
Step 1: Implement Product
public class ExcelDocument implements Document {
  @Override
  public void open() { System.out.println("Opening Excel Document."); }
  @Override
  public void close() { System.out.println("Closing Excel Document."); }
  @Override
  public void save() { System.out.println("Saving Excel Document."); }
}
Step 2: Create ConcreteCreator
public class ExcelDocumentCreator extends DocumentCreator {
  @Override
  public Document createDocument() {
    return new ExcelDocument();
  }
}
Key Takeaway

Adding a product only requires a concrete product and a concrete creator; no changes to existing clients or creators are necessary.

screens.title: Logger Factory activity — starter code
screens.subtitle: Implement the Factory Method for a logging system

narration.text: The chapter includes a hands-on activity: build a Logger Factory where logs can be written to different destinations, such as console or file. The starter code provides a Logger interface and two concrete loggers: ConsoleLogger and FileLogger. It also provides an abstract LoggerFactory with an abstract createLogger method and a logMessage utility that uses the created logger to write a message. Your task is to implement ConsoleLoggerFactory and FileLoggerFactory, plus fill in the Main class to instantiate and test both factories. This exercise reinforces the pattern: Logger is the Product, ConsoleLogger and FileLogger are ConcreteProducts, LoggerFactory is the Creator, and ConsoleLoggerFactory/FileLoggerFactory are ConcreteCreators. A key point is how FileLoggerFactory is constructed with a default file name used by FileLogger; this shows how creators can carry configuration for created products. When you implement the Main method, verify the console output and the FileLogger initialization message. A common mistake is to put file path logic into the application instead of the factory; prefer configuring the factory so the client remains simple. Logger Factory activity — starter code means use the logger example to practice defining product, concreteproducts, creator and concretecreators and to see how creators can own configuration for products.. In practical terms, implement the factory method for a logging system. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Practice pattern
keyIdea.text: Use the Logger example to practice defining Product, ConcreteProducts, Creator and ConcreteCreators and to see how creators can own configuration for products.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Logger Factory Activity
Starter Code: Product & ConcreteProducts
// Product Interface: Logger
public interface Logger {
  void log(String message);
}

// Concrete Products: ConsoleLogger, FileLogger
public class ConsoleLogger implements Logger {
  @Override
  public void log(String message) {
    System.out.println("Console Log: " + message);
  }
}

public class FileLogger implements Logger {
  private String fileName;

  public FileLogger(String fileName) {
    this.fileName = fileName;
    System.out.println("FileLogger initialized for: " + fileName);
  }

  @Override
  public void log(String message) {
    System.out.println("Writing to " + fileName + ": " + message);
  }
}
Starter Code: Creator
// Creator Abstract Class: LoggerFactory
public abstract class LoggerFactory {
  // The factory method
  public abstract Logger createLogger();

  // An operation that uses the created logger
  public void logMessage(String message) {
    Logger logger = createLogger(); // Get the specific logger
    logger.log(message);
  }
}

// Concrete Creators: ConsoleLoggerFactory, FileLoggerFactory
public class ConsoleLoggerFactory extends LoggerFactory {
  @Override
  public Logger createLogger() {
    return new ConsoleLogger();
  }
}

public class FileLoggerFactory extends LoggerFactory {
  private String defaultFileName;

  public FileLoggerFactory(String defaultFileName) {
    this.defaultFileName = defaultFileName;
  }

  @Override
  public Logger createLogger() {
    return new FileLogger(defaultFileName);
  }
}
Your tasks
  • Implement Main to instantiate ConsoleLoggerFactory and FileLoggerFactory and call logMessage.
  • Confirm console output and FileLogger initialization message.
  • Try adding a DatabaseLogger and DatabaseLoggerFactory to test extensibility.

screens.title: Common mistakes and practical tips
screens.subtitle: Avoid overuse, god factories, and keep interfaces focused

narration.text: The chapter warns about several common mistakes when applying the Factory Method. First, overuse: do not reach for this pattern if your application only ever needs a single product type or if creation logic is trivial and unlikely to change. Adding an abstract Creator and multiple factories adds complexity that may not pay off. Second, the 'God' factory anti-pattern: avoid creating a single factory class that knows how to construct all products. That centralizes too much responsibility and becomes hard to maintain. The Factory Method encourages a hierarchy of creators, each responsible for a specific product or family. Third, confusing Factory Method with a Simple Factory: remember the Factory Method uses inheritance and polymorphism rather than a switch on a string. Practical tips: keep the Product interface small and focused; let creators carry configuration needed for construction; and prefer composition over inheritance to reuse creation logic if appropriate. Finally, when testing, mock the Creator or Product interfaces to isolate behaviors. Ask yourself: does this refactor reduce modification points for future changes? If not, the added abstraction may be premature. Common mistakes and practical tips means don't over-abstract; avoid monolithic factories; keep interfaces focused and prefer multiple small creators to a single god factory.. In practical terms, avoid overuse, god factories, and keep interfaces focused. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Avoid these traps
keyIdea.text: Don't over-abstract; avoid monolithic factories; keep interfaces focused and prefer multiple small creators to a single god factory.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Pitfalls & Best Practices
Common Mistakes
  • Overuse when only one product exists.
  • Creating a single 'god' factory that knows everything.
  • Mixing product-specific APIs into the Product interface.
Best Practices
  • Keep Product interfaces minimal and stable.
  • Give each creator a focused responsibility and configuration.
  • Mock Creator or Product interfaces in tests for isolation.
Check your understanding

Identify one constructor call in your code that, if replaced by a Creator, would avoid editing multiple clients when adding a new type.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Core ideas to keep in mind

narration.text: Here are the essential concepts to retain. First, the Factory Method defines an interface for creating a Product but lets subclasses decide which ConcreteProduct to instantiate, enabling deferred creation. Second, the pattern's participants — Product, ConcreteProduct, Creator, ConcreteCreator — each have clear responsibilities: Product is the interface, Creator declares the factory method and may implement operations, and ConcreteCreators supply concrete instances. Third, the pattern supports the Open/Closed Principle: you extend by adding new ConcreteProducts and ConcreteCreators rather than modifying existing client or creator code. Remember also the tradeoffs: added abstractions and more classes. Finally, when choosing between a static factory and the Factory Method, prefer the simpler static factory when types are stable and choose Factory Method when you expect extension through polymorphism. Factory Method Pattern
Defines a method for creating objects and defers the exact class to subclasses.
Pattern Roles
Product, ConcreteProduct, Creator and ConcreteCreator each have focused responsibilities.
Open/Closed Principle
Add new product types by adding classes, not by modifying existing client code.
Takeaway

Use Factory Method to move construction into a polymorphic creator hierarchy so your codebase becomes easier to extend and maintain.

narration.text: Keep these practical rules front of mind as you apply the pattern. First, prefer small, focused Product interfaces so concrete implementations remain interchangeable. Second, let creators own construction concerns, including configuration necessary for product initialization. Third, resist building monolithic factories; create a ConcreteCreator per product or product family to keep responsibilities small. Fourth, when adding new product types, favor creating new ConcreteProducts and ConcreteCreators rather than modifying existing factories or clients. Finally, test by mocking creators or products to verify orchestration without constructing real resources. These reminders help you apply the Factory Method sensibly: gain extensibility and decoupling without unnecessary complexity.
